sec.title: Background
sec.p: AZD5863 is a bispecific T cell engager (TCE) with high affinity to CLDN18.2 and low affinity to cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3), designed to decrease its peripheral cytokine release potential, improve the therapeutic index, and maintain potent anti-tumor activity.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: AZD5863 was evaluated using CLDN18.2-expressing human cell lines alone or in co-cultures with human or cynomolgus monkey peripheral blood mononuclear cells to determine affinities, specificity, potency, and bystander killing activity. In vivo, AZD5863-mediated tumor growth inhibition and pharmacodynamics were evaluated in humanized mice or human CD3 transgenic mice implanted with CLDN18.2-expressing cancer cell lines.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: AZD5863 was shown to bind specifically to human and cynomolgus monkey CLDN18.2 and to CD3, with CLDN18.2 binding also conserved against the murine protein. AZD5863 mediated T cell-dependent anti-tumor activity against CLDN18.2-expressing lines, with potency significantly correlating with CLDN18.2 receptor density. Cytokine secretion induced by AZD5863, in vitro and in vivo, was lower compared with a CLDN18.2 TCE with higher affinity for CD3. AZD5863 mediated T cell-dependent bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells in the presence of CLDN18.2-expressing cells, in a mechanism partly dependent on interferon gamma (IFNγ), tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), and Fas ligand. In vivo, AZD5863 treatment resulted in potent tumor control in pancreatic, gastric, and esophageal models and enhanced engraftment of immune populations in a humanized model.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: AZD5863 mediates potent anti-tumor activity in vitro and in vivo, while inducing limited levels of cytokines. This work improves our understanding of the mechanism of action of affinity balanced TCEs and informs the design of a phase 1 trial testing AZD5863 in gastric, pancreatic, and esophageal adenocarcinoma (NCT06005493).

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: T cell engagers (TCE) are emerging as a next wave of immune-oncology agents to bring concrete treatment options in the hematological and solid tumors spaces, with recent noteworthy approvals in the latter. CLDN18.2 is a clinically validated target, and a mAb approach, zolbetuximab, was recently approved as a first-line treatment of CLDN18.2-expressing advanced unresectable or metastatic gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma patients. CLDN18.2-targeting approaches are therefore being actively pursued by many through a variety of therapeutic modalities.

This work describes AZD5863, a novel TCE targeting Claudin 18.2 and cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3), developed to treat patients with Claudin 18.2-positive gastric, pancreatic, and esophageal cancers. By designing AZD5863 with affinity balance, that is, with high affinity binding to Claudin 18.2 and low affinity binding to CD3, we aim to reduce potential cytokine release syndrome side effects.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE, OR POLICY

list-item.p: This work describes the potent efficacy of AZD5863 in preclinical mouse models and its bystander activity in in vitro cultures with heterogeneous Claudin 18.2 expression, providing insights into patient selection strategies to be incorporated into the clinical development of AZD5863 and other CLDN18.2-targeting agents.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: T cell engagers (TCEs) are multispecific antibodies designed to bridge T cells to cancer cells and induce the formation of an artificial immune synapse. This leads to T cell activation and redirection of cytotoxic activity against cancer cells bypassing the need for antigen presentation by the major histocompatibility complex. TCEs typically bind to the cluster of differentiation 3 (CD3) receptor in the T cell receptor/CD3 protein complex expressed on the surface of T cells and to a tumor-associated antigen (TAA) on the tumor cell surface.1 Beyond triggering direct killing of TAA-positive cells, cytokines such as interferon gamma (IFNγ) released by TCE-activated T cells can drive bystander killing of antigen-negative cancer cells and promote additional T cell recruitment into the tumor microenvironment.2

The most common adverse events observed with TCEs are associated with T cell activation, particularly cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome.3 Preclinical studies indicate that reducing the affinity to CD3 and increasing affinity to the TAAs effectively decreases peripheral T cell activation and cytokine production, potentially lowering the risk of CRS.4 5 In addition, TCEs engineered with low affinity to CD3 have improved biodistribution to the tumor microenvironment where TAAs are highly expressed.6

TCEs have shown clinical promise in the treatment of hematologic malignancies, such as acute lymphoblastic leukemia or multiple myeloma, where multiple drugs have been approved in recent years.7 However, the progress of TCEs on targeting solid tumors has been slower. One of the key challenges of targeting solid tumors with TCE approaches is the identification of TAAs that are restricted to cancer cells and avoid TCE targeting of healthy tissues which can result in on-target/off-tumor toxicities.8

CLDN18.2 is highly expressed in several types of cancer, including gastric, esophageal and pancreatic cancer, and its expression is maintained in metastases. It is present in about 70% of gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers (G/GEJCs).9 Aberrant expression has also been found in pancreatic cancer (pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC)); esophageal adenosarcoma; biliary tract cancer; and with less frequency in ovarian, colorectal, and non-small cell lung cancers.911 The role of CLDN18.2 in carcinogenesis and its correlation with other clinicopathological features remains unclear, but accumulating evidence does not point to an essential role for CLDN18.2 in tumor initiation and progression. The normal tissue expression of CLDN18.2 is highly limited to differentiated cells of the gastric epithelium where it is localized to tight junctions. Because of its restricted expression and high prevalence in the aforementioned tumor types, there is a growing interest in CLND18.2 as a biomarker for targeted therapies, particularly in G/GEJC and PDAC. Clinical proof of concept for CLDN18.2 targeting has been demonstrated in G/GEJC with zolbetuximab, a murine-human chimeric IgG1 antibody that binds CLDN18.2 and mediates tumor cell death through antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) and complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC). When combined with capecitabine and oxaliplatin (CAPOX) or folinic acid, fluorouracil, and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX), zolbetuximab showed improvements in progression-free survival as compared with placebo plus CAPOX or FOLFOX in randomized phase III trials12 13 leading to its approval in 2024 by the FDA for the first-line treatment of adults with locally advanced unresectable or metastatic human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-negative gastric or GEJ adenocarcinoma whose tumors are CLDN18.2 positive in combination with fluoropyrimidine- and platinum-containing chemotherapy. Other therapeutic modalities against CLDN18.2 are in clinical development such as ADCs and chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-Ts),14 15 and TCEs such as AMG910, a CLDN18.2 targeting TCE developed by Amgen but discontinued in 2022 following phase I clinical studies with no clinical data published to date.

In an effort to target gastric, GEJ, and pancreatic cancers, we have developed AZD5863, a TCE-targeting CD3 and CLDN18.2. AZD5863 has been designed to monovalently bind CD3 with low affinity via a Fab domain and to bivalently bind CLDN18.2 with high affinity with dual antibody variable heavy domains (VH) to potentially improve its therapeutic index. Here, we show that AZD5863 has specific binding to CLDN18.2 and CD3, induces potent CLDN18.2-dependent and T cell-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (TDCC) in vitro as well as bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells only in the presence of CLDN18.2-positive cells. In vivo, AZD5863 induces potent tumor control in both humanized and syngeneic tumor models and increases T cell levels in treated tumors. When compared with a high CD3 affinity TCE control, AZD5863 induces lower cytokine release in vitro and in vivo, which may translate to an improved therapeutic index in the clinic. AZD5863 is under a phase I clinical study in CLDN18.2-positive gastric, GEJ, esophageal, and pancreatic cancer patients in multiple clinical sites worldwide (NCT06005493).

sec.title: Cell lines and reagents
sec.p: All cells used in the experiments described in this article were kept in culture for a maximum of 2 months before starting new cultures from master vials. Cell lines were purchased from ATCC, DSMZ, or other commercial sources and grown in the recommended media. Short tandem repeat reauthentication tests were performed on receipt of cells and banking. Mycoplasma testing was performed on all cell lines prior to use using R&D MycoProbe Mycoplasma Detection Kit (R&D Systems). Cell line engineering and quantification of CLDN18.2 molecules per cell in human cancer cell lines and tumor samples were conducted as detailed in the online supplemental material.

sec.title: Affinity determination
sec.p: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) biosensor affinity and kinetic assessment experiments were performed at 25°C on Biacore 8K series instruments (Cytiva) using chips and reagents from Cytiva (Little Chalfont, UK). The running buffers were HBS-P+buffer (10 mM HEPES pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 0.05% Surfactant P20) which is a buffered saline based on HEPES (4-(2-hydroxyethyl)−1-piperazineethanesulfonic acid). Protein column chromatography columns and consumables were also supplied by Cytiva. EZ link Sulfo-NHS-LC-Biotin (p/n 21335) and streptavidin (p/n 21125) were from Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc. The jackfruit (Artocarpus integrifolia) seed lectin Jacalin was from Vector Labs (p/n L-1150).
Detailed affinity determination methods are included in the online supplemental materials.

sec.title: Flow cytometry
sec.p: For Claudin 18.2 detection, tumor cells were harvested with Accutase (ThermoFisher) or TryPLE (ThermoFisher) where required and washed with PBS followed by staining with Zombie NIR Live Dead (BioLegend) at 1/800 dilution in PBS for 20 min at 4°C. Cells were then washed with fluorecence activated cell sorting (FACS) staining buffer and stained with AZD5863 conjugated with Alexa Fluor 647 with the AlexaFluor Antibody labeling kit (ThermoFisher) according to manufacturer’s instructions at a saturating concentration of 5 µg/mL, for 1 hour at 4°C. Finally, cells were washed with FACS staining buffer and fixed with paraformaldehyde 4%. For receptor density measurements of human CLDN18.2, Quantum Simply Cellular anti-human beads (Bangs laboratories) were stained with AF647-AZD5863 at 5 ug/mL similarly to cells, and both cells and beads were analyzed on a FACSymphony (BD) flow cytometer using the same voltage settings. The QuickCal program (Bangs Laboratories) was used to establish a standard curve reference which was used to calculate receptor density on the cell surface of the cell samples. Data capture used the FACSDiva software (BD Biosciences RRID:SCR_001456), and data analysis was performed using FlowJo software (V.10.8 for Windows RRID:SCR_008520).

For the bystander killing, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were collected at the end of the assay and stained first with Zombie NIR Live Dead (BioLegend) at 1/800 in PBS for 20 min at 4°C, and then cells were stained with the following flow cytometry antibody cocktail in FACS staining buffer, for 1 hour at 4°C: CD4-PE (BD Biosciences Cat# 555347, RRID:AB_395752, 1/50), CD25-BUV737 (BD Biosciences Cat# 612807, RRID:AB_2916878, 1/200), CD45-BUV395 (BD Biosciences Cat# 563792, RRID:AB_2869519, 1/100), and CD8-BV650 (BD Biosciences Cat# 563821, RRID:AB_2744462, 1/50), CD69-APC (BioLegend Cat# 985206, RRID:AB_2922660, 1/100). For immunophenotyping from humanized in vivo models, the following antibody cocktails were used: anti-mouse CD45-BUV395 (BD Biosciences Cat# 567451, RRID:AB_2916597), anti-human CD45-BUV737 (BD Biosciences Cat# 748719, RRID:AB_2873123), anti-human CD8-BV605 (BD Biosciences Cat# 564116, RRID:AB_2869551), anti-human CD3e-RB545 (BD Biosciences Cat# 569198), anti-human CD4-PE-Cy7 (BioLegend Cat# 317414, RRID:AB_571959), and live-dead blue viability dye (ThermoFisher). Finally, cells were washed with FACS staining buffer, fixed with paraformaldehyde 4%, and analyzed using a BD Fortessa X20 or Symphony flow cytometers (BD Biosciences). For cell binding assays, serial dilutions of test and control antibodies were incubated with target cells in FACS staining buffer, starting at a concentration of 1 mM and diluted fourfold across 10 points, followed by washing with FACS staining buffer and staining with secondary antibody (Thermo Fisher Scientific Cat# A-21445, RRID:AB_2535862) at a final concentration of 4 ug/mL along with live/dead red fixable reagent (ThermoFisher) at 1/1000 in FACS staining buffer for 1 hour at 4°C. Finally, cells were washed with FACS staining buffer, fixed with paraformaldehyde 4%, and analyzed using a BD Fortessa X20 or Symphony flow cytometers (BD Biosciences).

sec.title: Immune cell assays
sec.p: Human PBMCs from anonymous healthy donors were isolated from leukocyte cones (National Health Service Blood and Transplant service) or purchased from Allcells. Leukocyte cones were washed with PBS, and blood was layered over Ficoll Paque-Plus as per manufacturer’s instructions and centrifuged at 400 g for 40’ at room temperature in a swinging-bucket rotor without brake. Then, PBMCs were recovered from the interface between plasma and Ficoll, washed two times in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), and red blood cells were lysed in ACK lysing buffer (ThermoFisher) as per manufacturer’s instructions. After counting, PBMCs were frozen at 5×106 cells per mL in cryo vials and stored in liquid nitrogen until required. Human T cells (effector cells) were isolated from PBMCs using the EasySep Human T cell enrichment kit (StemCell) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

For the T cell-dependent cytotoxicity assay (TDCC), target cells were collected by Accutase treatment as per manufacturer’s instructions and plated at 1.5×104 cells/well in 50 uL in a 96-well flat bottom plate in Roswell Park Memorial Institute (RPMI) 5% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and placed at 37°C, 5% CO2 for 3–4 hour to adhere. Isolated human PBMC or T effector cells were thawed at 37°C in a water bath and transferred into prewarmed 10 mL RPMI 5% FBS media. After one wash in media, PBMCs were counted and plated with the target cells at a density of 6×104 cells/well in 50 uL RPMI 5% FBS media for an effector:target ratio of 4:1, 1:1, 1:2, or 1:4, depending on the experiment. Test article AZD5863 or isotype control antibody was added in triplicates in a fourfold dose titration starting from 10 nM in 50 uL RPMI 5% FBS media, and control articles were added in triplicates at a concentration of 10 nM in RPMI 5% FBS media into experimental wells (ER). To calculate cytotoxicity levels, target+effector only (T+E) control wells were included. Plates were incubated for 48 hours at 37°C, 5% CO2. After 48 hours, supernatants were collected, and PBMCs were removed by washing twice with PBS. Cytotoxicity of target cells was measured using the Cell Titer Glo kit (Promega) as per manufacturer’s instructions and calculated from the luminescence values according to the following formula: Cytotoxicity (%) = 100-(ER/avg T+E)*100. Normalized cytotoxicity values were calculated and presented. For Incucyte TDCC assays, NUGC4-GFP cells were plated at a density of 1×105 cells per well in a 96-well flat bottom plate for 24 hours, prior to the addition of 4×105 PBMCs and increasing doses of AZD5863. Cells were incubated within an Incucyte SX5 (Sartorius) for 5 days, during which live images were acquired every 2 hours. NUGC4-GFP confluence was quantified as GFP area-per-well normalized to 2-hour timepoint. Where indicated, data was transformed to area under the curve (AUC).

For bystander assay, PaTu8988s (RRID:CVCL_1846) High sort CLDN18.2+(HS) and PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO (KO) were collected by TrypLE treatment as per manufacturer’s instructions. After counting, cells were washed once in warm PBS and then resuspended at 2×106 cells/mL in 37°C PBS. Labeling dyes carboxyfluorescein succinimidyl ester (CFSE) (2 µM, ThermoFisher) and CellTrace Violet (CTV) (2 µM, ThermoFisher) were prepared in prewarmed PBS and used to label PaTu8988sHS cells and PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO cells, respectively. Cells were incubated with CFSE or CTV dyes at a 1:1 vol ratio for 10 min at 37°C. Cells were then washed in warm RPMI 10% FBS media, counted, and then 1.2×104 total cells were seeded per well in 96-well flat bottom plates at specified ratios (HS:KO proportions: 100:0 (HS only), 70:30, 50:50, 30:70, 20:80, 0:100 (KO only)) in RPMI 10% FBS and placed at 37°C, 5% CO2 overnight. Human PBMC effector cells were thawed at 37°C in a water bath and transferred into 10 mL of RPMI 10% FBS media at 37°C. After one wash in RPMI 10% FBS media, PBMC were counted and plated with the target cells at a density of 6×104 cells/well in 50 µl RPMI 10% FBS media for an effector:target ratio of 4:1. AZD5863 was added in duplicate in a 10-fold 6-point titration starting from 10 nM in 50 µL RPMI 10% FBS media. After 3 days of culture, supernatants were collected for MSD analysis and PBMCs were collected into a new 96-well V-bottom plate. Then, target cells were collected using Accutase treatment for 15 min at 37°C and added to the PBMCs plate for flow cytometry staining and analysis. The assay was similarly conducted utilizing MDA-MB-231-CLDN18.2 or wild-type (WT, RRID:CVCL_0062). To investigate the mechanisms of bystander killing, the assay was conducted using MDA-MD-231-CLDN18.2 or WT cells at 30%:70% CLDN18.2+:CLDN18.2- ratio, in the presence or absence of 1 nM AZD5863 and with or without blocking antibodies for IFNγ (inVivoMab, used at 2 µg/mL), TNFα (Cell Signalling Technologies used at 2 µg/mL), or Fas Ligand (FasL) (R&D, used at 2 µg/mL). Cytokine secretion was evaluated in supernatants by Meso Scale Discovery (MSD, Rockville, USA) assays, according to manufacturer’s instructions. Standard curve calculations and cytokine concentrations were calculated using the MSD Workbench software.

sec.title: Mice and tumor challenge
sec.p: The animals were humanely treated and housed according to protocols reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of CrownBio or AstraZeneca (protocols AUP-22–17 and AUP-22–25). During the study, the care and use of animals were conducted in accordance with the regulations of the Association for Assessment and Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care. All analyses were performed blinded such that experimenters performing tumor measurements, sampling, and data analysis were unaware of the treatments administered. Power calculations were performed to determine appropriate group size for experiments using R. Length’s calculator16 Java Applets for Power and Sample Size (computer software) from http://www.stat.uiowa.edu/~rlenth/Power. Human xenograft tumors were established by subcutaneous (SC) injection. NUGC-4 (RRID:CVCL_3082) cells (5×106) were mixed with human PBMCs (1×106) in 0.1 mL of 50% Matrigel in PBS and inoculated in the right front flank of 6–8 week-old NSG (NOD.Cg-Prkdcscid Il2rgtm1Wjl/SzJ IMSR_JAX:005557) mice. Patu8988sHS (RRID:CVCL_1846) (1×107) and OE19 (RRID:CVCL_1622) cells (5×106) were suspended in 50%:50% Matrigel:PBS and inoculated in the right front flank of 6–8 week-old NSG (IMSR_JAX:005557) mice. For Patu8988HS and OE19 models, PBMCs from human healthy donors were stimulated for 3 days using T Cell TransAct (Miltenyi) before being briefly phenotyped to inject a cell suspension comprising 1×106 CD3+ T cells into the animals. Only one IV PBMC injection was conducted in the Patu8988HS and OE19 humanized models. MC38 expressing murine CLDN18.2 were generated as described above and implanted (1.5×106) into the right front flank of 6–8 week-old human CD3-transgenic C57BL/6 immunocompetent mice (Genoway). Animals were randomized as detailed in the online supplemental material.

For cytokine release studies, six female NCG mice (NOD-Prkdcem26Cd52Il2rgem26Cd22/NjuCrl RRID:IMSR_CRL:572) were used per group. Animals were randomly allocated into two groups according to body weights on day 0. Randomization was performed based on the “Matched distribution” method (StudyDirectorTM software, V.3.1.399.19). Mice were humanized by intravenous administration of human PBMCs (2×107/mouse in 0.2 mL in PBS) on day 0. On day 1 animals in group 1 were administered a control human IgG1 antibody, and animals in group 2 were administered AZD5863, both at 10 mg/kg. Test articles were administered intravenously. Four hours (4 hours) after test article administration, serum samples were collected from individual mice. The rate of tumor growth for each animal was estimated based on fitting each tumor’s growth curve to an exponential model as per the following equation:

where a and b are parameters that correspond to the log initial volume and growth rate, respectively. The model assumes the error terms are normally distributed. Statistical significance was assessed using Mann-Whitney t-test.

For in vivo PK study, six female BALB/c Nude mice were administered AZD5863 at 5 mg/kg via IV bolus on day 1. Blood samples were collected at the following time points: 0 hour (Pre-dose), 5 min, 5 hours, 24 hours, 48 hours, 96 hours, 168 hours, 240 hours, and 336 hours. At each sampling time point, 50 mL of blood was collected from the orbital venous plexus. Three mice were sampled at each time point, and groups of three mice were alternated in the time points sampled. Blood samples were left to clot at room temperature for 1 hour, and serum was collected and frozen at −80°C until further analysis for AZD5863 concentration. The bioanalytical assays for PK determination are detailed in the online supplemental material.

sec.title: Tumor dissociation and processing
sec.p: Tumors were excised from mice using scissors and placed in Miltenyi Gentlemacs C-tubes containing 2 mL of RPMI containing 1 mg Collagenase IV (Millipore Sigma C4-22-1G), 50 IU DNAseI (Millipore Sigma D5025), and 0.25 mg hyaluronidase (Millipore Sigma H6254), and processed on Miltenyi Gentlemacs tissue dissociators for 41 min. After dissociation, the reaction was quenched by adding 18 mL RPMI with 10% FBS (ThermoFisher A5256801) and 55 µM 2-mercaptoethanol (ThermoFisher 21985023). The resulting solutions were strained through a 70 µM cell strainer and counted, after which samples were resuspended in PBS containing 1% FBS and 2 mM EDTA.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The cell binding or TDCC potency for AZD5863 was determined by generating half maximal effective concentration (EC50) values using a nonlinear regression model (log agonist vs response – variable slope (four parameters)) in GraphPad Prism, V.8 (GraphPad Software). EC50 values are presented as mean±SD unless otherwise stated. The mean fluorescence intensity was used as a measurement of cell binding activity. The % cytotoxicity or cytokine production was used as a measurement of TDCC activity. Statistical significance evaluated using tests described in figure legends using GraphPad Prism, V.8 (GraphPad Software RRID:SCR_002798). For graphical depictions, data was sometimes normalized, taking the highest and lowest values per data set as 100 and 0%, respectively. Graphical depictions of data were performed using GraphPad Prism V.8 for Windows (RRID:SCR_002798).

sec.title: Data availability statement
sec.p: Data were generated by the authors and included in the article; any raw data are available on request from the corresponding author.

sec.title: AZD5863 binds specifically to CD3 and Claudin 18.2
sec.p: AZD5863 was designed as a 2+1 format TCE as depicted in figure 1A with two identical heavy chain variable (VH) regions, tandemly linked, binding to Claudin 18.2 and a fragment antigen binding (Fab) region binding to CD3. AZD5863 is a modified human IgG1, with knob-into hole heterodimerization mutations and, in order to abolish antibody effector functions, for example, ADCC, three mutations (L234A, L235A, G237A)1719 have been incorporated into the CH2 domains of both heavy chains. Affinity determination by SPR showed that AZD5863 binds with high affinity to human Claudin 18.2 (KD=0.1 nM) and with low affinity (KD=170 nM) to the human CD3δε heterodimer (figure 1B, C and online supplemental table S1). Additionally, AZD5863 showed binding to the commonly occurring M149L variant of human Claudin 18.2,20 to cynomolgus and murine Claudin 18.2, and to cynomolgus monkey CD3δε heterodimer (online supplemental figure 1B, C and table S1) with similar affinities to the human proteins (online supplemental table S1). In cell binding assays, AZD5863 showed binding to HEK293 cells engineered to express human, cynomolgus monkey, and murine Claudin 18.2 with comparable EC50 values and to Jurkat cells that express human CD3 but showed no binding to HEK293 cells engineered to express Claudin 18.1 or to non-engineered HEK293 cells (figure 1D, S1C, and S1D and online supplemental table S2).

caption.title: AZD5863 binds with low affinity to CD3 and high affinity to Claudin 18.2. (A) Schematic representation of AZD5863, a bispecific antibody with two VH-only antibody domains to Claudin 18.2 (orange) and one antibody domain to CD3 (δε heterodimer, blue-green) with Fc-disabling mutations (L234A, L235A, G237A). (B) AZD5863 binds to human CD3 (δε heterodimer) protein with an affinity of 170 nM in a surface plasmon resonance (SPR) assay (representative results from three independent experiments are shown). (C) AZD5863 binds to human Claudin 18.2 VLPs (virus-like particles) with an affinity of 0.1 nM in a SPR assay (representative results of two independent experiments are shown). The fully corrected binding data for both interactions were globally fitted to a 1:1 binding model to determine the KD using the Biacore Insight Evaluation Software (Cytiva). Light blue sensorgram trace represents the raw data and dark blue line the global 1:1 fit to that data. (D) Geometric mean fluorescence intensity (GMFI) of AZD5863 binding to cell surface–expressed human Claudin 18.2, Claudin 18.1, or to non-transduced HEK293 and Jurkat cells, determined by flow cytometry. Data from triplicates presented as mean ± SD. For EC50 determinations, antibody concentration, and GMFI, data were log transformed before analysis and fit using the log agonist versus response using Prism Software (GraphPad; representative results of three independent experiments). See also online supplemental figure S1. CD3, cluster of differentiation 3.

sec.title: AZD5863 induces T cell-mediated cytotoxicity of cancer cell lines in a Claudin 18.2 and CD3-dependent manner
sec.p: To evaluate the ability of AZD5863 to specifically kill tumor cells expressing Claudin 18.2, we used TDCC assays. Human or cynomolgus monkey PBMCs were co-cultured with HEK293 cells engineered to express human or cynomolgus monkey Claudin 18.2 or human Claudin 18.1 (with human PBMCs only). When exposed to AZD5863, PBMCs showed potent cytolysis of cells expressing CLDN18.2 but not CLDN18.1, demonstrating the cross-reactivity and specificity of AZD5863, respectively (online supplemental figure S2A, B). To further demonstrate that the activity of AZD5863 requires both the presence of CD3 and CLDN18.2, we incubated human PBMCs with AZD5863 in the presence or absence of HEK293 cells engineered to express human CLDN18.1. We observed minimal or null release of IL6 and TNFα in the supernatant of the co-culture assay in response to AZD5863 treatment or an isotype control antibody, whereas using a positive control such as lipopolysaccharide induced high levels of both cytokines (online supplemental figure S2C, D). Additionally, to demonstrate that AZD5863 induces T cell killing via CD3 binding, we used an incucyte in vitro assay, monitoring NUGC4-GFP tumor cell growth over the course of 5 days, in the presence of increasing doses of AZD5863 and with or without PBMCs in co-culture. By quantifying AUC over a range of AZD5863 concentrations (online supplemental figure S2E), as expected, we observed an increase in tumor cell growth inhibition with increasing doses of AZD5863 only in the presence of PBMCs, indicating that the TCE-induced cytotoxicity requires anti-CD3 to engage on T cells. Altogether, these data indicate that AZD5863 (i) induces specific T cell-mediated killing of CLDN18.2-expressing cells, (ii) is functionally cross-reactive to cynomolgus monkey CLDN18.2, (iii) induces low or no cytokine release in the absence of CLDN18.2-positive target cells, and (iv) induces effective cytotoxicity of tumor cells with the presence of both CLDN18.2 and CD3 being necessary. To assess the relative potency and variability of AZD5863 TDCC activity, we incubated the gastric cancer cell line NUGC4, which expresses endogenous levels of CLDN18.2, with PBMCs from multiple donors (n=7) and analyzed the cytolysis of NUGC4 cells and the release of relevant cytokines (IL2, IFNγ, IL6, and TNFα) into the assay supernatant. The cytolysis potency (EC50) of AZD5863 was comparable across all PBMC donors with an average of 26±11 pM (figure 2A) and was lower than the EC50 of any of the cytokines tested (figure 2B), indicating that AZD5863 is two- to six-fold more potent to induce cytolysis of CLDN18.2 positive cells than cytokine release.

sec.p: To ensure this higher cytolytic potency compared with cytokine release was not the result of a single time point assay read-out, we conducted a longitudinal analysis of AZD5863 potency in the same TDCC assay and profiled cytotoxicity, cytokine production, and T cell activation across several time points (2, 24, 48, 72, and 144 hours; online supplemental figure S3 and S4). AUCs for both cytolysis and cytokine release across all timepoint were calculated and plotted against each concentration (online supplemental figure S3). After normalization, we show that AZD5863 displays five- to 80-fold higher cytotoxic potency compared with cytokine release over time, similar to the single timepoint observation (figure 2C).

To understand the relationship between AZD5863 potency and CLDN18.2 expression levels, TDCC assays were performed across a panel of cancer cell lines expressing varying levels of CLDN18.2 (online supplemental figure S5). AZD5863 induced cytotoxicity on a range of cell lines starting from 700 up to 160 000 CLDN18.2 ABC, and its cytotoxic potency (EC50) significantly correlated with CLDN18.2 expression (p=0.0003), with higher levels of CLDN18.2 receptors resulting in higher potency of AZD5863 (figure 2D). To address whether the cell lines used in in vitro and subsequent in vivo studies present with clinically relevant levels of CLDN18.2 expression, we conducted CLDN18.2 quantification by mass spectrometry on tumor cell lines and on a gastric cancer patient cohort. Quantification of CLDN18.2 molecules per cell revealed that the cell lines used for our in vitro and in vivo studies span a clinically relevant range of CLDN18.2 expression (online supplemental figure S5B).

Finally, in order to recapitulate treatment conditions that may be more representative of the tumor microenvironment, we tested AZD5863 in TDCC assays with E:T ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4 (online supplemental figure S5C). Importantly, we observed a decrease in cytotoxicity at 48 hours with increasing number of tumor cells in the co-culture, with this effect being less prominent after 6 days of co-culture (online supplemental figure S5C).

sec.title: AZD5863 affinity balance grants better cytotoxicity and lower cytokine secretion potential compared with an AMG910 analog with higher CD3 affinity and lower CLDN18.2 affinity, in vitro and in vivo
sec.p: To investigate the impact of designing AZD5863 with a low affinity anti-CD3 and high affinity for CLDN18.2, we compared its cytotoxicity potency and cytokine secretion potential to an analog of AMG910 (AMG910a), a CLDN18.2 TCE with higher CD3 affinity and lower CLDN18.2 affinity (6.15 nM and 48 nM, respectively) (online supplemental figure S6 and table S3). In vitro, AZD5863 showed a marginally improved cytotoxicity compared to AMG910a in a TDCC assay with PBMCs and NUGC4 tumor cells (Cytotoxicity EC50s: AZD5863=21.5 pM; AMG910a=40.9 pM; figure 3A). Importantly, despite the increased cytotoxicity, AZD5863 induced lower levels of IFNγ, TNFα, and IL-6 secretion, compared with AMG910a (figure 3B). These data indicate that AZD5863 presents with better cytotoxicity and lower cytokine secretion than AMG910a, suggesting a better therapeutic index (figure 3C). Similarly, when AZD5863 was administered in vivo, in an NCG immunodeficient model humanized with human PBMCs, we observed significantly lower levels of IFNγ, interleukin 2 (IL2), TNFα, and IL6 in the animals’ serum, compared with AMG910a, 4 hours after dosing (figure 3D). Interestingly, IFNγ and TNFα levels driven by AMG910a in vivo peaked at 4 hours after dosing and subsequently diminished, with AZD5863-driven cytokine secretion remaining lower throughout the time course assessed (figure 3E).

sec.title: AZD5863 mediates bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells
sec.p: We next investigated whether AZD5863 can mediate bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells. To this end, we developed an in vitro bystander killing assay in which human PBMCs are co-cultured with PaTu8988s tumor cells (sorted for high CLDN18.2 expression, WT), and CLDN18.2-knock out (KO) PaTu8988s cells, at different WT:KO ratios, indicated in figure 4A. Each tumor cell line was labeled with a cell-tracking dye (PaTu8988s in CFSE and PaTu8988s KO in CTV) prior to seeding. Following 72 hours of co-culture with PBMCs, TDCC of WT or KO cells was assessed by flow cytometry (figure 4A), at each WT:KO ratio tested. As expected, no AZD5863-mediated TDCC of PaTu8988s KO cells was observed when these were cultured with PBMCs in the absence of PaTu8988s WT (figure 4B). However, in the presence of CLDN18.2 positive cells, AZD5863 induced TDCC of CLDN18.2 KO at all WT:KO ratios tested, indicating that AZD5863 can induce bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells, as a result of CLDN18.2-positive cells killing (figure 4B). In all PBMC donors tested, when AZD5863 was added at 10 nM, there was a significant difference in the TDCC of PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO at WT:KO ratios of 70:30, 50:50, 30:70, and 20:80, compared with the condition with only PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO cells (online supplemental figure S7A). The cytotoxic activity of AZD5863 on PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO cells when only KO cells were present was not significantly different from the untreated condition, in all PBMC donors tested (online supplemental figure S7A). As expected, AZD5863 induced T cell-dependent cytotoxicity of PaTu8988s cells alone or in co-culture with PaTu8988s CLDN18.2 KO at all ratios tested (online supplemental figure S7B).

sec.p: In line with our cytotoxicity results, we observed a dose-dependent upregulation of activation markers CD25 and CD69 on both CD8+ and CD4+ T cells from PBMCs co-cultured with WT and KO cells at all ratios tested or when cultured with WT cells alone but not when cultured with KO cells alone (figure 4C). Secretion of IFNγ, TNFα, and IL-6 was also triggered in a dose-dependent manner only when KO cells were co-cultured with WT cells (figure 4D). Furthermore, our cytotoxicity data were recapitulated using MDA-MB-231 tumor cells (CLDN18.2-negative) mixed with MDA-MB-231 cells which were engineered to express CLDN18.2 (MDA-MB-231-CLDN18.2, online supplemental figure S7C).

Using this system, we investigated whether IFNγ, TNFα, or the FAS-FASL axis may contribute to AZD5863-induced bystander killing by conducting the assay in the presence of blocking antibodies for either cytokine or for FasL. We observed that single or dual IFNγ and TNFα blockade, dual TNFα, and FasL, as well as triple blockade of IFNγ, TNFα, and FasL significantly reduced, but did not fully abrogate TDCC of CLDN18.2-negative cells (MDA-MB-231). These data demonstrate that the mechanism of bystander killing is multifactorial and partly involves signaling via IFNγ, TNFα, and FAS-FasL (figure 4E). Interestingly, single TNFα, dual TNFα and FasL, as well as triple blockade of IFNγ, TNFα, and FasL also significantly reduced TDCC of CLDN18.2-expressing cells (MDA-MB-231-CLDN18.2, online supplemental figure S7D).

All together, these data indicate that AZD5863 can trigger bystander killing of CLDN18.2-negative cells when CLDN18.2-expressing cells are present, supporting the activity of AZD5863 in patients with heterogeneous CLDN18.2 expression.

sec.title: AZD5863 mediates control in humanized and CD3-transgenic mouse models for CLDN18.2+ tumors
sec.p: Next, we investigated AZD5863 treatment in vivo, using mouse models for CLDN18.2+ tumors. We initially determined the serum concentrations of AZD5863 in vivo by analyzing BALB/c Nude mice after an intravenous bolus injection of 5 mg/kg AZD5863. Using bioanalytical methods which measured free and total AZD5863, the terminal elimination half-life of free AZD5863 was 135hours (5.6 days), and the terminal elimination half-life of total AZD5863 was 173 hours (7.2 days) (online supplemental figure S8A and table S4).

We next implanted immunodeficientNOD SCID Gamma (NSG) mice with CLDN18.2+ expressing cell lines NUGC4 (gastric cancer), OE19 (esophageal cancer), or PaTu8988sHS (pancreatic cancer). The mice were humanized either by mixing unstimulated human PBMCs with the tumor cells prior to implantation (NUGC4 model) or by intravenous injection of pre-activated human PBMCs (adjusted to inject 1×106 T cells) after tumor establishment (OE19 and PaTu8988sHS models). In the NUGC4 and OE19 models, AZD5863, dosed intraperitoneally (IP), led to a significant reduction in tumor volume, compared with Isotype control (figure 5A, B, individual mice growth curves in online supplemental figure S9A, B). Next, we explored intravenous and IP administration of AZD5863 in the NUGC4 model (online supplemental figure S8B), as well as compared SC to IP TCE administrations in the OE19 model (online supplemental figure S8C). Our data demonstrate that AZD5863 led to similar reduction in tumor volumes, regardless of route of administration. In the PaTu8988sHS model, AZD5863 treatment led to a significant decrease in tumor volumes when dosed at 0.02 mg/kg and 0.2 mg/kg, with tumor regressions observed at the higher dose (figure 5C, left, individual mice growth curves in online supplemental figure S9C). To address whether distinct levels of pre-existing T cell infiltration impact AZD5863-mediated tumor control, we assessed AZD5863 treatment of NSG mice bearing PaTu8988sHS tumors, humanized with increasing numbers of pre-activated T cells (figure 5C, right). Interestingly, AZD5863 mediated a significant decrease in tumor volume when the mice were humanized with 5×105 T cells, compared with mice that were not humanized. A further significant decrease in tumor volumes, with complete 3/10 tumor regressions, was observed with humanization with 1×106 T cells. There was no significant difference in tumor volumes when comparing non-humanized mice with mice that received 1×105 T cells (figure 5C, right). Similarly, no effect was observed on tumor growth when AZD5863 was administered in the absence of humanization in the OE19 model (online supplemental figure S8D). Next, we investigated whether AZD5863 treatment can impact immune cell recruitment in vivo by treating NSG mice bearing PaTu8988sHS with AZD5863 at two dose levels or with an isotype control. AZD5863 triggered a dose-dependent increase in CD45+, CD3+, CD4+, and CD8+ cells; as percentage of total live cells, 24 days following humanization, an effect that was significant when comparing 0.2 mg/kg AZD5863 to the isotype control (figure 5D) and was also found at an earlier timepoint (10 days post-humanization, online supplemental figure S8E). Similarly, peripheral human CD45+ cells, CD3+, CD8+, and CD4+ T cells were found to be significantly increased, as a proportion of live cells, at day 10 following humanization, in response to 0.2 mg/kg AZD5863 (online supplemental figure S8F).

sec.p: To investigate AZD5863 treatment in the presence of an endogenous anti-tumor immune response, we used immunocompetent transgenic human-CD3 (CD3δεγ) C57BL/6 mice and implanted these with MC38 tumor cells, engineered to express mouse CLDN18.2. Importantly, AZD5863 treatment at 5 mg/kg determined a significant decrease in tumor volumes in this model (figure 5E, left; individual mice growth curves in online supplemental figure S9D) and a significant decrease in the tumor growth rate at both 1 mg/kg and 5 mg/kg, compared with the isotype control (figure 5E, right).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Bispecific TCEs are emerging as a concrete therapeutic avenue for cancer treatment both in the context of hematological malignancies and more recently, solid tumors,21 with the US Food and Drug Administration recently approving Tarlatamab in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer, as a prominent example.22 There are many challenges associated with targeting solid tumors with TCEs, including effective tumor biodistribution, managing off-target and on-target off-tumor effects, CRS, and potential emergence of resistance mechanisms.23 To circumvent these challenges, several strategies are being investigated to design next-generation TCEs and optimize their clinical development plans, in the hope to yield durable responses and greater therapeutic index.

In line with these efforts, we designed AZD5863, a 2+1 format CLDN18.2 and CD3-binding TCE, which presents with low affinity to CD3 and high affinity to CLDN18.2. CLDN18.2 is an emerging target for cancer therapy, given its restricted expression to the tight junctions of normal epithelial cells of the gastric mucosa and aberrant expression in gastric, pancreatic, and GEJ cancers.9 24 Indeed, CLDN18.2-targeted therapeutic approaches, including CAR-T cells and zolbetuximab alone or in combination with chemotherapy, have demonstrated clinical benefit in gastric cancer.1214

As the other isoform of CLDN18, CLDN18.1, is instead restricted to the lung epithelium,25 we showed that AZD5863 is uniquely specific to CLDN18.2 and not CLDN18.1, which eliminates the risk of off-target effects in healthy lung. Interestingly, AZD5863 cytotoxic activity in vitro significantly correlated with the levels of CLDN18.2 cell surface receptors, indicating that target expression correlates with TCE potency, and, accordingly, AZD5863 was not active on cell lines lacking CLDN18.2 expression. At the same time, we observed activity over a large range of CLDN18.2 levels (between 700 and 160 000 receptors), indicating that AZD5863 might be able to direct T cells to mediate killing of tumor cells with low expression levels of CLDN18.2 in patients. AZD5863 was shown to bind specifically to the CD3δε heterodimer with an affinity of 170 nM and to CLDN18.2, with an affinity of 0.1 nM. Such low affinity to CD3 is hypothesized to result in a favorable toxicity profile, as modulation of CD3 affinity in TCEs has been shown to improve biodistribution to TAA+tumors and to yield low cytokine secretion.6 26 Additionally, AZD5863 was shown to be cross-reactive to murine and cynomolgus monkey CLDN18.2.

As mentioned above, designing next-generation TCEs with low affinity for CD3 is a key strategy to decrease their toxicity potential.21 AZD5863 was shown to be more potent in inducing cytolysis of CLDN18.2 positive cells than in inducing release of cytokines including IFNγ, IL6, and TNFα, all involved in CRS.27 This specificity remained true over time, as we observe the same in a longitudinal TDCC assay, confirming the effect is not the result of a single timepoint read-out. While changing the E:T ratio in favor of tumor cells resulted in decreased AZD5863 potency, these in vitro assays are closed system and cannot accurately recapitulate the effect that AZD5863 might have on T cell recruitment. Direct comparison of AZD5863 to an analog of AMG910, a CLDN18.2 TCE with higher affinity to CD3 and lower affinity to CLDN18.2, which was discontinued in 2022 following phase I clinical studies, showed better potency and lower cytokine secretion potential in vitro. Importantly, these findings were also observed in vivo, in NSG mice, in which AMG910 analog yielded a peak of cytokine secretion at 4 hours after dosing, while AZD5863-driven cytokine secretion remained low, up to 24 hours after dosing. These results are in line with other reports, in which CD20 or HER2 targeting TCEs with lower affinity to CD3 were shown to induce lower cytokine levels in the serum of cynomolgus monkeys, compared with high-affinity counterparts, without impacting efficacy.6 26 AZD5863 might therefore present with a more favorable toxicity profile in the clinic, with lower potential of inducing CRS, compared with other CLDN18.2-targeting TCEs.

Solid tumors can have heterogeneous TAA expression which presents an additional challenge for TCEs.2 Here we modeled heterogeneous target expression in vitro by mixing distinct ratios of tumor cells that were either positive or negative for CLDN18.2 expression, in a TDCC assay. Interestingly, AZD5863 mediated T cell-dependent killing of both TAA+ and TAA- cells, as long as at least 20% of tumor cells in the culture were CLDN18.2+, while TAA- cells were not killed in the absence of CLDN18.2+ cells. Similar patterns were observed for T cell activation and cytokine secretion, indicating that AZD5863 has the potential to mediate potent anti-tumor activity in patients with heterogeneous CLDN18.2 expression, via triggering of bystander killing of TAA- cells.

IFNγ and TNFα were previously shown to play a role in bystander killing of antigen loss variants in mouse models of cancer.28 FasL is known to be upregulated by TCE-activated T cells,29 with FAS-FasL interactions being a known mechanism of lymphocyte-mediated anti-tumor immunity.30 Therefore, we investigated the role of IFNγ, TNFα, and FasL in mediating the observed bystander killing effect, either alone or in combination with blocking antibodies. We observed that blocking all three pathways reduced AZD5863-mediated bystander killing but did not fully abrogate it, indicating that bystander activity is partially dependent on these pathways, but that other factors may also contribute, such as ICAM-1 pathway, as previously shown2 or effector molecules or cytokines such as granzyme-B, perforin, and IL2. Deeper mechanistic studies are required to fully delineate the individual factors involved.

In vivo, AZD5863 mediated potent, dose-dependent, anti-tumor activity against CLDN18.2+ tumors in multiple humanized models as well as in a syngeneic human CD3-transgenic mouse model. Of note, in the syngeneic model, no complete regressions were observed, an effect which we hypothesized to be likely driven by the insurgence of mouse anti-human anti-drug antibodies in this fully immunocompetent system. Efforts to overcome challenges associated with TCE clinical development for solid tumors include the evaluation of a variety of dosing strategies, such as testing of step-up dosing and SC administration, with the aim of achieving higher drug exposure while minimizing the risk of adverse events.31 Importantly, AZD5863 retained potent tumor control when administered using different routes, including SC injection, suggesting that this method of administration could be viable in the clinic to improve safety, without compromising on TCE activity.

Interestingly, in the humanized PaTu8988sHS mouse model, we observed a dose-dependent increase in intratumoral CD45+ cells and T cell subsets, in response to AZD5863, indicating that increasing doses of TCE result in a greater number of T cells within the tumors. Increased tumor T cell infiltration has also been observed in uveal melanoma patients treated with Tebentafusp.32 Intratumoral T cell proliferation or recruitment from the periphery could be individually or jointly responsible for increased tumor T cell levels, but additional studies are required to determine which of these mechanisms is predominant in preclinical models and in patients.

One important aspect that remains to be explored is the extent to which prolonged exposure to AZD5863 may lead to emergence of resistance mechanisms, such as upregulation of checkpoint molecules and T cell exhaustion. Of note, a recent publication demonstrated that a low-affinity CD3 TCE could drive sustained T cell activation with reduced immune exhaustion, compared with a counterpart with higher CD3 affinity,33 suggesting that AZD5863 low CD3 affinity may be similarly beneficial to T cell function. Nevertheless, it has been previously discussed that T cell activation following TCE treatment is expected to be characterized by the upregulation of activation and exhaustion markers that modulate T cell function, which may open up opportunities for combination therapies such as co-stimulation or immune-checkpoint inhibition approaches.34

In conclusion, the data presented show that AZD5863 presents with potential for improved safety, due to its low CD3 affinity, and potential for lower cytokine secretion. AZD5863 is currently being investigated in a phase I first-in-human clinical study in CLDN18.2+GC/GEJ/PDAC patients (NCT06005493).
